_about: Glossary for the modules and workbook. Built by tools/make-glossary.py.

entries.def: Passage of a drug from where it is given (for example the gut) into the blood.
A known active is a compound proven to hit the target. A decoy is assumed inactive. Mixing them tests whether a method can pick out the actives.
What the body does to a drug: how it gets into the blood (A), where it goes (D), how it is chemically changed (M) and how it is removed (E). Often written ADMET to add toxicity.
Computer systems that perform tasks that normally need human intelligence. The About page states that an AI coding assistant helped to write the software.
Lining up two sequences so that matching positions sit in the same column, with gaps where one has extra residues.
A deep-learning program that predicts protein structures from sequence.
AMPA receptors carry fast excitatory signals in the brain. GluA2 and GluA3 are two of their subunits. NTD is the N-terminal domain. The homology module uses their real structures as the example.
A compound that differs from another by a small change, for example a methyl group replaced by chlorine.
Two meanings in the site. In screening: area under the ROC curve, from 0.5 (random) to 1 (perfect). In ADME: area under the concentration–time curve, the total exposure to a drug.
A free, widely used docking program.
A number stored for each atom in a crystal structure that tells how much the atom seems to move or be uncertain. Large values mean floppy or poorly defined regions.
The set of genes the list is compared against in enrichment. The choice changes the result a lot and must be stated.
How often a node lies on the shortest path between two other nodes. High values mark bridges.
A tight layer of cells that limits what can pass from blood into the brain. Some drugs need to cross it, some must not.
A table that scores how likely one amino acid is to replace another during evolution. Used to score alignments.
A plot of polar surface area against cLogP. Compounds in the white are predicted to be absorbed by the gut, and in the yolk to also enter the brain.
A backbone drawn through only the central carbon atom of each residue. A simplified model.
Using computers to help find and improve medicines: choosing targets, finding compounds, predicting how they bind and how they behave in the body.
A compound chosen to go forward to more detailed testing.
Enzymes that interconvert CO₂ and bicarbonate. Celecoxib is reported to inhibit some of them, which is why they appear as celecoxib targets outside the inflammation picture.
What you decided in each module, saved in your browser and passed to the next module.
The COX-2 selective drug used as the reference (known active) throughout the project. Its crystal structure bound to COX-2 is PDB 3LN1.
A widely used force field for proteins.
CH3 is a methyl group, CH2 a methylene, OH a hydroxyl (alcohol or phenol), CH2OH a hydroxymethyl, OCH3 a methoxy group, NCH3 an N-methyl group. Several of them are metabolic soft spots.
An observed relationship between sequence identity and expected structural difference between related proteins (1986). Higher identity means a smaller expected RMSD.
Two atoms that are closer than is physically possible. A pose with clashes is not believable.
Clearance (CL) is the volume of blood cleared of drug per unit time. Volume of distribution (V) relates the amount in the body to the blood concentration.
How near a node is, on average, to all other nodes.
The highest concentration of a drug in the blood (Cmax) and the time at which it is reached (Tmax).
A non-protein helper (a metal ion or a small molecule such as haem) that an enzyme needs to work.
A collection of compounds (real or virtual) that is screened.
An enzyme that makes the chemical signals (prostaglandins) behind pain and inflammation. It is the target in the project. COX-1 (PTGS1) is a related enzyme that protects the stomach lining.
A drug designed to block COX-2 more than COX-1, for example celecoxib, rofecoxib, etoricoxib.
A method that finds structures by imaging frozen molecules with an electron microscope.
Plain-text file formats for tables (CSV) and structured data (JSON). The site exports your record in these.
A family of liver enzymes that chemically change most drugs (phase I metabolism). CYP2C9 handles celecoxib.
The number of links a node has.
How different the chosen compounds are from each other. Eight look-alikes test one idea eight times.
The molecule that carries genes. Genes are the blueprints for proteins.
A computer experiment that predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein pocket (the pose) and estimates how well (the score).
A rough estimate of binding strength. More negative is better. It is the least reliable part of docking, so use it with the pose and interactions.
The short name of the course author, Dr Nur 'Ainun Mokhtar (Universiti Teknologi MARA).
A laboratory test that measures the amount of a protein in a sample with antibodies.
Moving atoms to relieve clashes and huge forces before dynamics starts.
Asks whether your list of genes contains more members of a pathway than expected by chance.

entries.more: EF = (actives in top n / n) / (actives overall / library size).
entries.def: How many times more known actives are in the top part of a ranking than expected by chance. 1 means no better than random.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction. Many drugs are enzyme inhibitors.
The settling period before measuring, in which temperature, pressure and density reach their targets. Its frames are discarded.
A docking setting (in AutoDock Vina) for how thoroughly the program searches. Higher is slower and more thorough.
PDB: protein or complex coordinates. PDBQT: PDB with charges and atom types, for AutoDock. SDF: one or more molecules with 3D coordinates. FASTA: a protein sequence. See Appendix D.
A string of 1s and 0s that records which structural features a molecule has. Used to compare molecules quickly.
The set of equations and parameters that give the forces between atoms (bonds, angles, charges, van der Waals). Examples: CHARMM, AMBER.
A very small molecule, often used as a starting point that chemists then grow.
The chance of finding a particle at distance r from another, relative to random. Sharp peaks mean order (a solid), low wide peaks mean a liquid.
The cost of opening or extending a gap in an alignment. Gaps belong in loops, not inside helices or strands.
The short official name of a gene, for example PTGS2 (COX-2), TNF (tumour necrosis factor), AKT1 and STAT3 (signalling proteins).
Databases linking genes to diseases, each with a score (a relevance score in GeneCards, a gene–disease association score in DisGeNET). Used to collect disease genes.
Predicted passage across the gut wall (high or low).

entries.full: Gene Ontology / Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes
entries.def: GO classifies genes by process, function and location. KEGG is a collection of pathway maps. Both are used as lists of gene sets in enrichment analysis.
A free, widely used molecular dynamics program.
The percentage of simulation frames in which a particular hydrogen bond is present.
An iron-containing helper molecule built into some proteins, including COX-2. It is a cofactor, not part of the protein chain.
The time for the blood level of a drug to fall by half.
The number of groups that can give (HBD) or accept (HBA) a hydrogen bond.

entries.more: For an acid: fraction neutral = 1 / (1 + 10^(pH − pKa)). For a base: 1 / (1 + 10^(pKa − pH)).
entries.def: Links pH and pKa to the fraction of a compound that is ionised. Only the neutral form crosses membranes easily.
A compound that looks active in a screen. Hits still need confirming.
Building a 3D model of a protein from its sequence, using the known structure of a related protein as a template.
A well-connected node. Hubs are leads to test, not proven targets: well-studied proteins also look like hubs.
A strong electrical attraction between a hydrogen on one atom (donor) and a nitrogen or oxygen on another (acceptor), about 2.7 to 3.3 Å long. A key way drugs hold on to proteins.
Oily parts of the ligand and protein packed together, away from water. Many small contacts add up.
The statistical test behind simple enrichment: the chance of drawing at least k pathway genes in a list of n, when the pathway has K genes among N in total.
The concentration of a compound that reduces the activity of a target by half. Smaller means more potent.
A code that names one item, for example a PDB ID such as 3LN1 or a participant ID.
A compound that reduces the activity of an enzyme or other target.
A measure of binding strength: the concentration at which half of the target is bound. Smaller means tighter binding.
Pocket residues known to matter for binding (for COX-2: HIS90, GLN192, ARG513).
The binding constant of an inhibitor for an enzyme. Smaller means tighter binding.
A confirmed, promising compound that is improved by chemistry to become a drug candidate.
A simple force between two atoms: attraction at a distance and strong repulsion up close.
A small molecule that binds a protein. In docking, the drug or compound being fitted into the pocket.
Docking score divided by the number of heavy atoms (kcal/mol per atom). It stops large molecules looking better just because they are large.
Searching for compounds that resemble a known active, by 2D similarity or 3D shape.
Methods that hold bond lengths fixed, which allows a 2 fs time step.
How much a compound prefers oil to water, on a log scale. High values mean greasy. cLogP is the calculated value.
logS is log10 of solubility in mol/L. ESOL is a simple equation (Delaney 2004) that estimates it from cLogP, weight, rotatable bonds and aromatic proportion.
A simulation that moves every atom according to the forces on it, step by step, to see how a system behaves over time.

entries.full: Molecular mechanics with generalised Born (or Poisson–Boltzmann) and surface area
entries.def: A quick end-point method that estimates binding free energy from simulation frames. It gives a rough ranking, not an accurate binding energy, and usually leaves out entropy.
Data made up or generated for teaching, not measured or calculated by a real program. The site labels them wherever they appear.
Programs that build homology models, including side chains and refinement.
The mass of a molecule in daltons (Da). Larger molecules are usually absorbed less well.
Common salt. A simulation box is usually given 0.15 M NaCl to mimic the salt in the body.
The network pharmacology tutorial protocol by Dr Nur 'Ainun Mokhtar that the network and molecular dynamics modules follow.
The toxic metabolite of paracetamol. In overdose it damages the liver.
Mapping all the targets of a drug, the genes of a disease, and the interactions and pathways that connect them, to see how a drug may act as a whole.
A method that finds structures of proteins in solution from the magnetic behaviour of their atoms.
In a network, a node is a protein (a dot) and an edge is an interaction (a line).
A painkiller that also reduces inflammation by blocking COX enzymes, for example ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac.
NVT keeps the number of particles, volume and temperature fixed. NPT keeps the pressure, not the volume, fixed. They are the two equilibration stages before production.
The fraction of an oral dose that reaches the blood unchanged.

A p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if nothing is going on. When many pathways are tested some look significant by chance, so p-values are corrected (Benjamini–Hochberg). The corrected value is the FDR or q-value. q < 0.05 is the usual limit.
Structures that often give false positives in lab tests, for example by reacting with the assay rather than binding the target. They are removed or treated with suspicion.
A laboratory test of how well a compound passes through an artificial membrane by passive diffusion.
A chain of molecular events, such as a signalling route, that a group of genes takes part in.
The public archive of 3D structures of proteins and other molecules. Each entry has a four-character ID, for example 3LN1 (COX-2 with celecoxib).
A trick to avoid edges: a particle leaving one side of the box re-enters on the opposite side.
A measure of acidity. The stomach is about pH 1.5 to 2, blood 7.4.
The set of features (for example hydrogen-bond donors, aromatic rings) in a given 3D arrangement that a molecule needs to bind a target.
Phase I reactions (oxidation, hydrolysis) expose or add a reactive group. Phase II reactions attach a polar group (for example glucuronic acid) so the kidney can remove it.
The pH at which half of a group is ionised. Acids are mostly neutral below their pKa, bases above it.
A curve that levels off. A protein RMSD that plateaus suggests the structure has settled.
The per-residue confidence score (0 to 100) of an AlphaFold prediction. Above 90 is very high, below 70 is low.
The cavity on a protein where a ligand binds. Its shape and chemistry decide which molecules fit.
A drug acting on more than one target.
A predicted position and orientation (and shape) of a ligand in the pocket.
A recorded or predicted contact or functional link between two proteins. A PPI network draws proteins as dots and these links as lines.
The part of a simulation that is analysed.
The hands-on practice notebook: a whole CADD project from question to conclusion, with automatic checks and a report. For use within this course only; do not enter real data.
Whether a group on a molecule carries an extra hydrogen (and charge) at a given pH. Histidine in particular can change, which changes the hydrogen bonds it can make.
A measure of how compact a protein is. A steady value means the protein keeps its overall shape.
A plot of the backbone angles φ and ψ of each residue. Real proteins fill certain allowed regions. Good models have over 90% of residues in the favoured region.
The organisation and website (rcsb.org) through which PDB entries are searched and downloaded.
An open-source chemistry toolkit used to compute the molecular properties and 3D shapes behind the modules.
Docking the ligand that is already in a crystal structure back into it, to check that the protocol can reproduce the known pose. An RMSD of 2 Å or less is the usual aim.
Units in which the particle size and energy are set to 1, so simple model systems apply to many substances.
A known active drug run through the same method, so that new compounds have something to be compared with.
An independent repeat of a simulation from different starting velocities. One run is one sample.
One amino acid in a protein chain. Written as a three-letter name plus a number, for example HIS90 or ARG513.

An amino acid is written by a three-letter code and its position in the chain: HIS90 is the histidine at position 90, ARG513 the arginine at 513. Codes: Ala, Arg, Asn, Asp, Cys, Gln, Glu, Gly, His, Ile, Leu, Lys, Met, Phe, Pro, Ser, Thr, Trp, Tyr, Val. COX-2 numbering follows the usual literature, 14 to 15 higher than in the PDB file.
How sharp an experimental structure is. A smaller number is better: below 2.5 Å is good, above 3.5 Å is poor.

entries.more: RMSD = √( Σ d² / N ), where d is the distance between matching atoms and N the number of atoms.
entries.def: A measure of how far one set of atoms is from another, in Å. Used to compare a docked pose with the crystal pose, a model with the true structure, or a simulation frame with the start.
How much each residue moves around its average position during a simulation. Loops and chain ends usually move most.
A graph of true positives against false positives as you move down a ranked list. A good method rises steeply.
Single bonds that can rotate freely. Many of them make a molecule floppy and harder to absorb.
A rule of thumb for oral drugs: molecular weight ≤ 500, cLogP ≤ 5, hydrogen-bond donors ≤ 5, acceptors ≤ 10. Breaking two or more makes poor absorption more likely.
How small changes in a molecule's structure change its activity.
The core ring system or skeleton of a molecule. Compounds with the same scaffold are structurally similar.
The series of filters that cut a large library down to a short list, with the number of compounds left after each.
The region of the protein in which the docking program looks for poses. It should cover the whole pocket with a margin, but not be far larger.
The local shapes of a protein chain: α-helices, β-strands and loops (coil).
The share of positions where two aligned sequences have the same amino acid. Above about 40% the model is usually good, below 30% (the twilight zone) the alignment is unreliable.
Laying one molecule on another in 3D and measuring how much of their volumes overlap.
A line of text that describes a molecule, for example CC(=O)O for acetic acid.
A part of a molecule that enzymes attack readily, for example an aromatic methyl group or an ester.
The uncertainty of a mean. Neighbouring frames of a simulation are correlated, so the error is estimated from blocks, which gives a larger and more honest value.
A database of known and predicted protein–protein interactions with a confidence score from 0 to 1. A cut-off of 0.7 is the usual "high confidence".
Searching by fitting compounds into the 3D structure of the target (docking).
A ten-question survey that gives a usability score from 0 to 100.
Free web tools that predict drug-likeness and ADME properties from a molecule.
Web tools that predict likely protein targets of a compound: the first from its similarity to known ligands (with a probability), the second by fitting it to 3D pharmacophores.

entries.more: Tc = shared features / (features in A + features in B − shared features).
entries.def: A number from 0 to 1 that says how similar two molecules are from their fingerprints (lists of structural features). 1 means identical.
The molecule in the body that a drug is meant to act on, usually a protein such as an enzyme or receptor.
The known structure that a homology model is built from.
Algorithms that keep the temperature (thermostat) or pressure (barostat) of a simulation near a target.
How far in time the simulation advances each step, usually 1 to 2 femtoseconds. Too large and the simulation breaks.
A common simple model of the water molecule used in simulations.
The surface area (Å²) of the polar atoms (N, O and their hydrogens). High values hinder crossing cell membranes.
The saved positions of all atoms at many time points.
The university where the site was created.
The main database of protein sequences and annotation. IDs look like P35354.
A second rule of thumb for oral absorption: polar surface area ≤ 140 Å² and no more than 10 rotatable bonds.
The standard method for moving atoms forward one time step from their forces.
Programs that check whether the amino acids of a model sit in suitable environments (buried or exposed).
Using a computer to rank or filter a large library of compounds to find a few worth testing.
A method that finds a protein's structure from how a crystal of it scatters X-rays.
A unit of length: 0.1 nanometre (10⁻¹⁰ m). A typical chemical bond is 1 to 1.5 Å long.
The energy change on binding, in kcal/mol. More negative means tighter binding.
